Quant finance for derivatives came a long way from simplistic delta hedging to AI driven "deep hedging". My lectures notes from Oxford earlier this year capture the link between Greeks based hedging and "statistical hedging", and how following down this path leads to "learning to trade" with AI.

But it doesn't have to be full Deep Hedging all the time.

"Statistical Hedging" in particular is a decidedly simple but effective method of managing portfolios of derivates - essentially, the idea is to "regress" (in a consistent way) portfolio returns vs hedging instrument returns. Greeks are not required.

If that's too bold of a step, "parameter hedging" is a compromise which lets you choose how much of each Greek to hedge based on the covariance of risk factors vs transaction cost of your hedging instruments.

Followed through faster than expected: tested it this weekend. Weekly NIFTY short strangle, 2019-2026, ~390 cycles, delta bands in the Whalley-Wilmott spirit vs never-hedge vs daily, measured spreads and STT, execution at next open so overnight gaps stay unhedged.

On the wing-capped structure we actually run, a pre-registered 1-lot band improved the weekly P&L 5th percentile ~11% at no mean cost. Real, but under our adoption bar. Tighter bands did more (~35% tail improvement for ~15% of the mean), with one catch: at our size, whole-lot execution makes any band tighter than half a lot identical to daily hedging. Band granularity turns out to be a function of book size.

The clean split was naked vs winged: on a naked version, daily hedging improved the tail ~40%. Your suggestion lands hardest exactly where it's designed for. Our takeaway: the wings we already carry are the pre-paid static version of the same intertemporal protection, bought once at entry instead of chased daily through spreads.

The corner solution survived, but with a measurement behind it instead of a shrug. Thank you for the push.

Statistical hedging changes the measurement technique. It doesn't necessarily change the measurement object.

Whether the hedge comes from Greeks, regression, or deep learning, the real question is whether the model is learning downstream price relationships or the asset architecture that generates them.

The interesting spread isn't between parameter hedging and AI. It's between models that optimize statistical relationships and models that detect whether capital dependency is accelerating or decelerating relative to the payoff surface they're trying to hedge.

Very interesting perspective, Hans Buehler.
 
I completely agree that statistical hedging offers a remarkably elegant alternative to traditional Greek-based approaches.
 
One aspect that we have been investigating is that, on production desks, the best statistical hedge is not always the best operational hedge.
 
Two hedge portfolios may deliver very similar out-of-sample risk reduction, yet have dramatically different turnover, support stability and implementation costs.
 
We recently observed that explicitly optimizing these operational objectives reduced portfolio turnover by more than 8× compared with a classical Top-K OLS hedge while maintaining strong out-of-sample hedging performance.
 
I wonder whether this "operational layer" could naturally complement statistical hedging or even Deep Hedging for real production workflows.
